subject: Computing
source: National Curriculum KS2 Computing (variables, repetition and selection, designing and debugging programs); Scratch game-making sequence adapted from the school's Drive Scratch Game Maker resources (Y7-Y9 computing overview) | Spring 1 2027 (lessons 5 to 9, v3): Tarbiyyah Primary computing long-term plan 2023-24 Year 5 Spring 1 (Selection in Physical Computing; Secure Your Secrets), NCCE Teach Computing based; MakeCode micro:bit simulator

lessons.title: Variables: boxes that store information
objectives: Explain that a variable stores a value which can change
Use 'set' and 'change by' to update a variable
Trace the value of a variable through a short algorithm

keywords.def: a named box that stores a value which can change
the information stored in a variable
give a variable a starting value
add to or take away from a variable

starter: Bismillah. Say what an if-then-else does.
A game shows 'Score: 0'. Where does the computer remember the score?

teach.heading: A variable is a labelled box
bullets: The label is the name: score.
The value can change; the name stays.
teach.note: Use real boxes or a drawn box with a sticky note. Write score on the label and 0 inside. Change the number inside. Ask what stayed the same and what changed. Misconception: pupils think a variable name and its value are the same thing.

teach.heading: Set and change
teach.note: Act it out: pupils hold a whiteboard with the variable name and a number; you give instructions and they update. Ask: after set score to 0, change by 3, change by 2, what is score? (5).

teach.heading: Trace it
teach.note: Show a trace table with a column per line of the algorithm and a row for the value. Teach pupils to fill it in line by line. This is the foundation for trace tables later in secondary computing.

teach.heading: Variables in real life
teach.note: Ask pupils to give their own examples of something that changes and a computer must remember. Example: the number of steps counted by a fitness watch.

practice: set score to 5, change score by 3, change score by -2. What is score? (6)
set lives to 3, change lives by -1 twice. What is lives? (1)
What is the variable name and what is the value in: set coins to 10?
independent: Complete 4 trace tables for algorithms with 'set' and 'change' blocks.
Write an algorithm to keep score in a game where you earn 10 points for a star and lose 5 for a rock.
Design a variable box diagram for a game: choose 3 variables, name them and give each a starting value.
exit: set x to 4, change x by 6. What is x?
lessons.homework: Find two places on a device or game where a number changes. Name the variable and describe when it changes.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use physical boxes and counters; give a template trace table. Stretch: trace an algorithm containing a repeat loop that changes a variable each time.

lessons.title: Variables in Scratch: score and lives
objectives: Use set and change blocks to update a score
Show a variable on the stage and test it

keywords.def: the button in Scratch that creates a new variable
makes the variable's value visible on the stage
a variable that all sprites can use

starter: Bismillah. set score to 2, change score by 5. What is score?
What stays the same in a variable: the name or the value?
Why might a game need a lives variable?

teach.heading: Make a variable
bullets: Name it score; choose 'For all sprites'.
teach.note: Share the screen and make the variable step by step. Pupils follow on their own machines. Explain that a name like score tells us what the variable is for, so choose names that make sense.

teach.heading: Start at zero
teach.note: Show what happens if you forget to set score to 0: the score continues from last time. Misconception: pupils think Scratch resets variables automatically; it does not.

teach.heading: Change the score
teach.note: Build a clicker game: click the star sprite to add 1 to the score. Run it and click five times. Ask for predictions: what will the score be after 10 clicks? Check.

teach.heading: Lives and sensing
bullets: If touching the rock: change lives by -1.
teach.note: Preview the selection with variables. Do not build all of it now. Ask pupils what blocks they will need and in what order. Connect to selection from Year 4.

practice: Which block puts the score back to 0 at the start of the game?
What happens to the score if the sprite is clicked 7 times and each click changes score by 2? (14)
Name two good variable names for a game and say what each is for.
independent: Build a click game: a sprite appears at a random place and each click adds 1 to score.
Add a second variable called 'clicks' that counts every click even when the sprite is missed.
Test the game and write what the score and clicks are after you click 10 times.
exit: Why do we set the score to 0 when the green flag is clicked?
Which block changes a variable by adding a number?
lessons.homework: Improve the click game at home: make the sprite move to a new place each time it is clicked, and send a screenshot.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a half-built project with the variable already created and the blocks to arrange. Stretch: make each click worth 2 points and the score show on the stage in a large font.

lessons.title: Loops and conditions: forever, if and repeat until
objectives: Use 'forever' with 'if' to keep checking something
Use 'repeat until' to repeat until a condition is true
Explain the difference between a count-controlled and a condition-controlled loop

keywords.def: a loop which never stops until the program ends
a loop which stops when its condition becomes true
a sensing block that checks if sprites meet

starter: Bismillah. How do you make a sprite move 10 steps five times without writing the block five times?
set coins to 3, change coins by 2. What is coins?
What does an if block need before it can decide?

teach.heading: Counting loops
teach.note: Recap repeat from Year 3 with a quick square. Ask pupils how they would know how many times to repeat if they did not know the number in advance.

teach.heading: Repeat until
bullets: The loop stops when the condition is true.
We do not need to know how many.
teach.note: Demonstrate a sprite moving 5 steps repeat until touching the edge. Change the starting position and show the loop still works. Misconception: pupils think the loop stops immediately when the condition is first checked; it checks every time round.

teach.heading: Forever and if
bullets: if touching star: change score by 1.
teach.note: Build a catch game: a basket sprite moves with the arrow keys; inside a forever loop an if block checks touching star. Explain that a loop with a condition inside is how games check what is happening. Show what happens without the forever loop (the check only happens once).

teach.heading: Choosing the right loop
bullets: Know when to stop: repeat until.
teach.note: Give three scenarios and ask which loop fits: draw a hexagon, walk until you reach the wall, keep checking for key presses. Take answers using thumbs signals.

practice: Which loop would you use to make a sprite walk until it touches a wall?
Which loop would you use to draw a pentagon (5 sides)?
A game must always check if the player touches an enemy. Which loop? (forever)
independent: Build a sprite which moves across the stage until it touches the edge, then says 'Done!'.
Build a catch game where the basket moves left and right and score increases when it touches the falling star.
Test the game and debug any problems; write one change you made.
exit: Which loop stops only when a condition becomes true?
Why does the 'if touching' block need to be inside a forever loop?
lessons.homework: Think of a game you play. Write which actions would need a forever loop and which would need repeat.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a screenshot of the finished script to compare with theirs and label the loops with colour. Stretch: make the falling star start at a random place at the top each time.

lessons.title: Project: design, build and test a catching game
objectives: Design a game using a plan with sprites, variables and rules
Use variables, loops and selection together
Test, evaluate and improve the game

keywords.def: plan what your program will do
decide how well something works and how to improve it
what happens when something occurs in the game

starter: Bismillah. Name the three kinds of loop block we have used.
What should a game do when lives reach 0?

teach.heading: Design first
bullets: Who or what is the player?
What do you catch or avoid?
What are the variables and rules?
teach.note: Show a design template: sprites, variables, rules, extras. Model filling it in for a fruit-catching game with dates. Explain why designers plan before building. Tidy and careful work is part of excellence (ihsan).

teach.heading: Build in steps
teach.note: Decompose the project into steps (callback to Year 3) and display them. Pupils should test after each step. Encourage them to save their project often.

teach.heading: Test with a checklist
bullets: Does the score go up when caught?
Does the game end at 0 lives?
teach.note: Give a checklist to tick off. Explain that a good tester tries unexpected things too, such as holding two keys. Typical bug: the score keeps rising while the item is touching the player; fix with a move-back or hide.

teach.heading: Evaluate
bullets: Ask a friend to play your game.
teach.note: Teach evaluation sentences: 'My game works well because... To improve it I would...'. Encourage honest and gentle peer feedback. Give a few minutes for pupils to play each other's games via shared links.

practice: Design on screen: choose three variables for the game (score, lives, time) and give each a starting value.
Write the rule for losing a life in the form IF ___ THEN ___.
Plan three steps for building the game in the order you would do them.
independent: Complete the design template for your own catching game.
Build and test your game with at least one variable, one loop and one if block.
Fill in the evaluation: two things that work and one improvement.
exit: Name one variable in your game and say what it does.
What is one bug you fixed and how did you find it?
lessons.homework: Add one improvement to your game (a new level, a timer, or sounds) and write one sentence about how it changes the game.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a starter project with sprites and backdrop; give sentence starters for the design and evaluation. Stretch: add a second type of falling object that takes points away.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Selection in physical computing and Secure Your Secrets
lessons.title: Secure your secrets: passwords, personal information and phishing
lessons.bigQuestion: A message says 'You have won a tablet! Click here and type your password.' What would make you suspicious?
objectives: To understand how to keep personal information secure and spot a phishing message
successCriteria: All: name three pieces of personal information to keep private
Most: spot two warning signs in a phishing message
Some: explain what to do and who to tell when a message looks suspicious
lessons.crossCurricular: PSHE: keeping safe and asking for help

keywords.def: facts that identify you, like your address or password
a fake message that tries to trick you into giving information
protected and safe
a secret that unlocks your account

hook.text: A message says 'You have won a tablet! Click here and type your password.' What would make you suspicious?
hook.a: You did not enter a competition; it asks for a password; it rushes you: all signs of phishing.

islamicLink.text: Islam teaches us to check news before we act on it: Allah says that if someone untrustworthy brings you news, verify it (al-Hujurat 49:6). Online, we check a message before we click.

starter.q: Which password is strongest? A) 123456 B) ali2015 C) RiverLampCarrot
What is a loop?
Who should know your password?
What should you do if something online worries you?

teach.heading: Personal information
bullets: Photos that show where you live
teach.note: These stay private. In Teams, use your first name only and never post your login in the chat.

teach.heading: What is phishing?
bullets: A fake message pretending to be real
teach.note: Bait: prizes, scares ('your account will close'), or a friend's name.

teach.heading: Warning signs
bullets: Odd spelling or a strange link
teach.note: Sort the messages.

cards: Teacher's homework post in your class Team
Message from your parent at home

teach.heading: What to do
bullets: Tell a parent or your teacher
They can report and delete it
teach.note: School staff never ask for your password.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: A message from 'Teams Support' asks for your password to 'fix your account'. What do you do?
options: Do not reply and tell a trusted adult
check.why: Real support never asks for a password; clicking can also be unsafe.

practice.q: Find two warning signs: 'URGENT!!! Your acount will be deleted. Type your password here.'
practice.a: Urgency and a request for the password (also the spelling 'acount').
practice.model: Teacher reads it aloud and underlines: 'URGENT' (rushing you), 'acount' (spelling mistake), 'type your password' (asks for a secret).

practice.q: Is your favourite colour personal information to keep private?
practice.a: Not usually: it does not identify you or unlock anything.

practice.q: Who do you tell about a phishing message?

independent.q: Core: Read the three messages on the worksheet. Mark each 'safe' or 'phishing' and give one reason.
independent.a: 1 phishing (prize and password), 2 safe (lesson reminder), 3 phishing (urgent link).

independent.q: Extend: Write a 'Secure your secrets' rule card with 4 rules in the portal response box.
independent.a: For example: never share passwords; check before clicking; first name only in Teams; tell a trusted adult.

independent.q: Stretch: Write a reply plan for a friend who has clicked a phishing link.
independent.a: Tell a parent now, change the password with a parent, tell the teacher, do not click again.

exit.q: Phishing is... A) a hobby B) a fake message that tricks you C) a strong password
exit.a: B) a fake message that tricks you
options: A fake message that tricks you

exit.q: Name one warning sign of phishing.
exit.a: For example: asks for a password, rushes you, too good to be true.

lessons.homework: Show a parent the four warning signs and together check that your school account password is strong.
lessons.send: SEND: messages read aloud with signs pre-highlighted. EAL: suspicious, urgent, link, private. Stretch: explain why phishing messages often use fear.

Phishing messages worksheet (pupil PDF; all messages invented by the school)

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Selection in physical computing and Secure Your Secrets
lessons.title: Selection: if... then rules
lessons.bigQuestion: Every morning you choose: coat or no coat? What question do you ask yourself first?
objectives: To understand how selection lets a program choose what to do using a condition
successCriteria: All: say the condition and the action in an if... then rule
Most: write if... then... else rules for everyday situations
Some: decide whether a condition is true or false for given inputs
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: comparing numbers (greater than, less than)

keywords.def: a program choosing what to do
a question that is true or false
if the condition is true, then do this
what to do when the condition is false

hook.text: Every morning you choose: coat or no coat? What question do you ask yourself first?
hook.a: 'Is it cold or raining?' That question is a condition; the choice is selection.

starter.q: Phishing is a... A) fake message B) game C) loop
What does a loop do?
What is an algorithm?
starter.a: A set of steps in order.

starter.q: Is '5 is bigger than 3' true or false?

teach.heading: Choices in programs
teach.note: Examples: a game checks if you touched the edge; a door opens if it senses someone.

teach.heading: If... then... else
teach.note: Condition: a question with a true or false answer.

teach.heading: Condition cards
teach.note: Unplugged: pupils hold up T or F on whiteboards.

model.problem: IF the number is more than 10 THEN clap ELSE stamp. The number is 7.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: IF the time is after Maghrib THEN put on the light ELSE keep it off. It is after Maghrib. What happens?
check.why: The condition is true, so the THEN part runs.

practice.q: IF score is 10 or more THEN say 'Well done' ELSE say 'Try again'. Score is 12.
practice.model: Teacher: condition 'is 12 at least 10?' Yes, true, so the THEN part: 'Well done'.

practice.q: Write an if... then... else rule for a plant: water it or not.
practice.a: IF the soil is dry THEN water it ELSE leave it.

independent.q: Core: Complete the condition cards worksheet: 6 rules, decide true or false and the action for each.
independent.a: Answers on the teacher key (one per card).
independent.model: Teacher completes card 1 aloud with the four model steps.

independent.q: Extend: Write three if... then... else rules for a robot helper at home.
independent.a: For example: IF the bin is full THEN empty it ELSE check tomorrow.

independent.q: Stretch: Write a rule with 'and': IF it is a school day AND it is 8:30 THEN log on to Teams. When is it false?
independent.a: False on a weekend, or on a school day at any other time.

exit.q: A condition is... A) always true B) a question that is true or false C) a loop
exit.a: B) a question that is true or false
options: A question that is true or false

exit.q: When does the ELSE part run?

lessons.homework: Write two if... then... else rules you follow at home (for example before going out).
lessons.send: SEND: T and F cards with pictures. EAL: if, then, else, true, false. Stretch: a rule with 'or'.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Selection in physical computing and Secure Your Secrets
lessons.title: A simulated micro-controller: button input, LED output
lessons.bigQuestion: Microwaves, washing machines and alarm clocks all have tiny computers inside. What do their buttons tell them?
objectives: To understand how a micro-controller program links an input to an output
successCriteria: All: name the input and the output on a micro:bit
Most: program button A to show an icon
Some: use buttons A and B to choose different outputs
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: electrical circuits, switches and bulbs (Year 4)

keywords.def: a tiny computer inside a device
information going in, like a button press
what the device does, like lighting LEDs
an on-screen copy of a real device

hook.text: Microwaves, washing machines and alarm clocks all have tiny computers inside. What do their buttons tell them?

starter.q: When does the ELSE part run?
Is a keyboard an input or output?
Is a screen an input or output?
Write an if... then rule for a doorbell.
starter.a: IF the button is pressed THEN ring.

teach.heading: Inside everyday devices
bullets: A micro-controller is a tiny computer
teach.note: Show the micro:bit picture: buttons A and B, 25 LEDs, sensors.

teach.heading: Inputs and outputs
teach.note: We will not use the speaker (no music).

teach.heading: MakeCode
bullets: Input blocks: on button A pressed
teach.note: Share screen; no login is needed. The simulator on the left acts like a real micro:bit.

code.text:
on button A pressed
  show icon (tick)
on button B pressed
  clear screen
code.output: Press A: a tick lights up. Press B: the LEDs go off.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: In 'on button A pressed, show icon', which part is the input?
check.why: The button press goes in; the icon on the LEDs is the output.

practice.q: Program button A to show a tick.
practice.a: on button A pressed: show icon (tick).
practice.model: Teacher drags 'on button A pressed' from Input and 'show icon' from Basic, chooses the tick, clicks A on the simulator.

practice.q: Program button B to clear the screen.
practice.a: on button B pressed: clear screen.

practice.q: What is the output in your program?

independent.q: Core: Make a 'yes / no' answer box: A shows a tick, B shows a cross, A+B clears.
independent.a: on A: tick; on B: cross; on A+B: clear screen.
independent.model: Teacher builds A and B, pupils add A+B.

independent.q: Extend: Use 'show LEDs' to design your own 5 by 5 picture of a crescent moon or a star for button A.
independent.a: Any correct show LEDs pattern on button A.

independent.q: Stretch: Use 'show number' and a button to count presses. Which block stores the count?
independent.a: A variable: set count to 0; on A: change count by 1, show number count.

exit.q: An LED lighting up is... A) an input B) an output C) a condition
Name one input on a micro:bit.
exit.a: Button A, button B, light sensor or temperature sensor.

lessons.homework: Find one device at home with a micro-controller. Write its inputs and outputs.
lessons.send: SEND: block screenshots to copy. EAL: input, output, press, show. Stretch: count presses with a variable.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Selection in physical computing and Secure Your Secrets
lessons.title: Selection with sensors
lessons.bigQuestion: How does a street light know when to switch on?
objectives: To understand how a sensor reading and a condition decide what a device does
successCriteria: All: name the light and temperature sensors on a micro:bit
Most: use if... then... else with a light reading
Some: choose and justify a threshold value for the condition
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: light and dark (Year 3) and thermometers

keywords.def: a part that measures the world, like light or heat
a true or false question the program checks
the value where the decision changes
try it with different inputs to check

hook.text: How does a street light know when to switch on?
hook.a: A light sensor measures how dark it is; below a threshold, the light turns on.

starter.q: An LED is an... A) input B) output
When does ELSE run?
Which block runs code when button A is pressed?
What does a simulator do?
starter.a: Copies a real device on screen.

teach.heading: Sensors as inputs
teach.note: In the simulator, drag the light slider to change the reading.

teach.heading: Light-controlled night light
bullets: Check the light again and again
teach.note: 'forever' keeps checking.

code.text:
forever
  if light level < 50 then
    show icon (small diamond)
  else
    clear screen
code.output: When it is dark (below 50) the LEDs light; when bright they go off.

teach.heading: Choosing a threshold
teach.note: Model with the slider.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: 'if light level < 50 then show icon'. The light level is 120. What happens?
check.why: 120 is not less than 50, so the condition is false and the else part runs.

practice.q: Build the night light and test with the slider.
practice.a: forever: if light level < 50 then show icon else clear screen.
practice.model: Teacher builds it, then tests at 10 (icon shows), at 50 (clear, as 50 is not less than 50) and at 200 (clear).

practice.a: So the micro:bit keeps checking the light, not just once.

independent.q: Core: Make a temperature warning: if temperature > 25 show a sun icon, else show a tick. Test with the slider.
independent.a: forever: if temperature > 25 then show icon (sun-like) else show icon (tick).
independent.model: Teacher swaps the light block for the temperature block in the night light script.

independent.q: Extend: Write a test table: three temperatures, what you expect, what happened.
independent.a: For example 20: tick, tick; 26: sun, sun; 25: tick, tick.

independent.q: Stretch: Explain why 25 is a sensible threshold for a 'too warm' room.
independent.a: Most rooms feel comfortable around 18 to 22 °C; above about 25 °C feels too warm.

exit.q: A street light uses which sensor? A) temperature B) light C) button

exit.a: The value where the decision changes.

lessons.homework: Name two devices at home that use a sensor to decide something (for example a fridge light, an oven thermostat).
lessons.send: SEND: script screenshots and a slider guide. EAL: sensor, light level, temperature, threshold. Stretch: use 'and' for a light and temperature condition.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Selection in physical computing and Secure Your Secrets
lessons.title: Design and build a device; selection quiz
lessons.bigQuestion: If you could build one helpful device for your home with a micro:bit, what would it do?
objectives: To understand how to design, build and test a device that uses selection
successCriteria: All: write the input, condition and output for a device
Most: build and test the device in the simulator
Some: debug it using a test table and improve it
lessons.crossCurricular: Islamic Studies: the five daily prayer times
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: a reminder that helps a family pray on time

keywords.def: plan what something will do before making it
a machine made for a job
the steps the device follows
find and fix mistakes

hook.text: If you could build one helpful device for your home with a micro:bit, what would it do?

starter.q: 'if temperature > 25'. Temperature is 25. True or false?
Which block keeps checking a sensor?
What is a threshold?
starter.a: The value where the decision changes.

starter.q: Name one warning sign of phishing.
starter.a: Asks for a password, rushes you, too good to be true.

teach.heading: Choose a device
bullets: Prayer-time reminder (button shows the next prayer)
teach.note: No sound blocks: outputs are LEDs and text.

teach.heading: Design first
teach.note: Fill the design frame before any blocks.

teach.heading: Build, test, debug
teach.note: Same debugging cycle as in Year 4.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: Your night light never turns on, even in the dark. First thing to check?
check.why: If the condition is never true (for example 'light level < 0') the output never runs.

practice.q: Fill the design frame for a night light.
practice.a: Input: light sensor; condition: light level < 50; output: show LEDs; else clear.
practice.model: Teacher fills the night light row aloud, linking each box to a block.

practice.q: For the prayer reminder, what is the input and the output?
practice.a: Input: button A; output: scrolling the next prayer time.

independent.q: Core: Design, build and test your chosen device in MakeCode. Share the project link in the portal.
independent.a: A working device with input, condition and output, tested.
independent.model: Teacher builds the first block of the night light from the design frame.

independent.q: Extend: Add a test table with three tests and results.
independent.a: Three tests with expected and actual results.

independent.q: Stretch: Improve the device (for example two thresholds, or button B for another prayer).

exit.q: Selection quiz (portal, 4 questions): conditions, true or false, input and output.
Big question: what would your device do and which sensor or button does it use?
exit.a: For example: my night light uses the light sensor and lights the LEDs when it is dark.

lessons.homework: Show your device to your family in the simulator and explain its input, condition and output.
lessons.send: SEND: the night light as a starter project to adapt. EAL: design frame with picture labels. Stretch: reaction timer with a variable.
